subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease and a diastolic rumble at the apex undergoes right- and left-heart catheterization. The wedge pressure recorded with a balloon-tipped catheter in the pulmonary artery is noticeably higher than the pressure measured at end-diastole within the left ventricle.
question: Which of the following correctly explains this catheterization finding?

options.text: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure always exceeds LV end-diastolic pressure in normal hearts
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure approximates right atrial pressure rather than left atrial pressure
In mitral stenosis, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure exceeds LV end-diastolic pressure because of obstruction at the mitral valve
The wedge pressure overestimates LV end-diastolic pressure because the Swan-Ganz catheter measures pulmonary arterial systolic pressure
LV end-diastolic pressure normally exceeds pulmonary capillary wedge pressure due to active ventricular relaxation

explanation_correct: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is a good approximation of left atrial pressure, except in mitral stenosis, where PCWP > LV end-diastolic pressure. The stenotic mitral valve obstructs flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, so left atrial (and thus wedge) pressure rises above the LV end-diastolic pressure. PCWP is measured with a pulmonary artery (Swan-Ganz) catheter.

explanation_incorrect.A: Normally PCWP approximates left atrial pressure and closely tracks LV end-diastolic pressure; a sustained gap is abnormal and points to mitral stenosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: PCWP approximates left atrial pressure, not right atrial pressure; right atrial pressure is measured directly from the right heart chambers.
explanation_incorrect.D: PCWP is obtained by balloon occlusion of a pulmonary artery branch and reflects left atrial pressure downstream of the occlusion, not pulmonary arterial systolic pressure.
explanation_incorrect.E: In a normal heart, LV end-diastolic and wedge pressures track each other closely; the documented wedge-to-LV gradient in this patient reflects mitral obstruction, not ventricular relaxation dynamics.

educationalObjective: PCWP approximates left atrial pressure; in mitral stenosis, PCWP exceeds LV end-diastolic pressure because of obstruction at the mitral valve.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A pulmonologist explains regional blood flow regulation to a class. She notes that within a portion of the lung with poor ventilation, the local vessels constrict and redirect blood toward better-ventilated regions, and she emphasizes that this response is unique to the pulmonary circulation.
question: Why is this pulmonary response described as unique among the organs?

options.text: Because the lungs use myogenic stretch responses of the afferent arteriole
Because in other organs, hypoxia causes vasodilation rather than vasoconstriction
Because the lungs rely on sympathetic vasoconstriction for temperature regulation
Because alveolar hypoxia causes vasodilation, matching perfusion to ventilation
Because the lungs autoregulate via tubuloglomerular feedback

explanation_correct: The pulmonary vasculature is unique in that alveolar hypoxia causes vasoconstriction, so that only well-ventilated areas are perfused. In other organs, hypoxia causes vasodilation. This reversed response redirects blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward better-oxygenated regions of the lung.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myogenic stretch-dependent responses of the afferent arteriole are a kidney autoregulation mechanism, not a pulmonary one.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sympathetic vasoconstriction for temperature control is the key skin mechanism, unrelated to alveolar hypoxia.
explanation_incorrect.D: This reverses the pulmonary response: alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels so perfusion matches ventilation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tubuloglomerular feedback is a renal autoregulation mechanism and has no pulmonary counterpart.

educationalObjective: Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction — a unique response, since hypoxia vasodilates vessels in other organs.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 60-year-old man with progressive dyspnea undergoes right-heart catheterization with a Swan-Ganz catheter. The balloon is inflated in a distal branch of the pulmonary artery, and a wedge pressure is recorded.
question: Which value represents the normal resting range for pulmonary capillary wedge pressure?

options.text: 4-12 mm Hg
Less than 5 mm Hg
Less than 8 mm Hg
Approximately 25 mm Hg
120/80 mm Hg

explanation_correct: The normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 4-12 mm Hg, reflecting its role as a good approximation of left atrial pressure. It is measured with a pulmonary artery (Swan-Ganz) catheter. Values above this range suggest elevated left-sided filling pressures, as seen in left heart failure or mitral stenosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: A pressure below 5 mm Hg corresponds to a right atrial value on the normal pressure diagram, far below the normal wedge range.
explanation_incorrect.C: Less than 8 mm Hg corresponds to the right ventricular diastolic value, not the wedge pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Approximately 25 mm Hg corresponds to normal pulmonary artery systolic pressure, well above the wedge range.
explanation_incorrect.E: 120/80 mm Hg is the normal systemic arterial blood pressure, several-fold higher than cardiac filling pressures.

educationalObjective: Normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 4-12 mm Hg and approximates left atrial pressure.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A renal physiologist measures blood flow to an organ while varying perfusion pressure over a wide range and finds that flow remains nearly constant. She attributes this autoregulation to two distinct intrarenal mechanisms acting at the level of the afferent arteriole and the tubule.
question: Which factors determine autoregulation in this organ?

options.text: Local vasodilatory metabolites: NO, CO2, and decreased O2
Local metabolites during exercise: CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, and K+
Sympathetic vasoconstriction as the most important mechanism
Myogenic (stretch-dependent) response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback
Alveolar hypoxia-induced vasoconstriction

explanation_correct: Renal blood flow is autoregulated by two mechanisms: the myogenic (stretch-dependent) response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback. Together they keep renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate nearly constant over a wide range of perfusion pressures.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vasodilatory local metabolites NO, CO2, and decreased O2 determine autoregulation in the heart, not the kidney.
explanation_incorrect.B: CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, and K+ are the exercise-related metabolites that regulate skeletal muscle blood flow.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sympathetic vasoconstriction is the dominant mechanism for temperature control in the skin, not the kidney's autoregulation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alveolar hypoxia-induced vasoconstriction is the unique pulmonary autoregulatory response, not a renal mechanism.

educationalObjective: Renal autoregulation depends on the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback.
